texts.facts: The present complaint has been filed by the complainant against the accused under section 138 Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter referred as the "Act"). Complainant's Version: 1. The complainant avers that complainant is a Private Limited Company duly incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956 and interalia dealing in Food Products in whole sale and Shri Vijit Aggarwal is one of its directors. Shri. Vivek Verma has been working in the complainant company as a Manager and was duly authorized to file the present complaint by virtue of a Board Resolution dated 05.03.2019 and is competent to sign and file the present complaint and therefore, the present complaint has been signed, filed and presented by the said Vivek Verma, Manager. After agreeing with all the terms and conditions, the accused used to purchase Food products from the complainant company from time to time and had been making payments regularly to the complainant for the value of the goods purchased from the complainant. The accused further placed the orders for the purchase of Food Products before the complainant i.e. invoice no.TI/001358 dated 20.07.2018 for amounting Rs. 3,75,347.00, TI/001565 dated 10.08.2018 amounting Rs. 7,42,576.00, TI/001850 dated 04.09.2018 amounting to Rs.1,37,068.00 and DN/0059 dated 26.12.2018 amounting to Rs.85,621.00. The food products against the aforementioned invoices were sent by the complainant, which were duly received by the accused. The said Food products were duly sent by the complainant through M/s MLT Transport Company, 16B, New Qutub Road, Delhi110006, vide GR no.12206 dated 20.07.2018 and G. R. no.12504 dated 04.09.2018 and G. R. No.12382 dated 11.08.2018. Thereafter, on making persistent requests by the complainant, the accused made some part payments and further the accused has failed to make the outstanding payment within the stipulated period as per the agreed terms and conditions. Then, instead of making balance payment, the accused had sent some Cans back in the month of October, 2018 i.e after eight months of the purchase/receipt of the same, even without any intimation. On inspection, all the returned Cans were spreading smell and found in a very bad/damaged condition and the same cannot be redressed or sold to another party. C.C. No.1727/19 Dated 17.01.2023 Pages 2 The said Cans were kept by the accused in the poor storage and even most of the cans were heavily dented and leaked. As per the terms and conditions, as agreed, no replacement would be given after one month of purchase/receipt of the goods. Thereafter, the complainant sent a letter dated 27.12.2018 through speed post, apprising the accused with all the facts, with the request to lift the said goods within seven days from the receipt of the aforesaid letter and to make the outstanding amount. The said letter was duly received by the accused on 29.12.2018 and thereafter, the accused neither lifted the said returned goods nor made the outstanding amount to the complainant. Therefore, as per the statement of accounts maintained by the complainant, there was a closing balance of Rs. 1240,666/ including interest of 2 per cent per month and other charges, as per agreed terms and conditions against the accused. Thereafter, as per the general trade and practice as prevailed in the market and on making persistent requests by the complainant, the accused in order to discharge his liability issued one cheque bearing 18. Sharma Carpets (2009) 2 Scc on 17 January, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/15751217/ 2 no.640958 amounting to Rs. 1240666/ dated 08.01.2019 drawn on State Bank of India, Old Railway Road, Jalandhar District Jalandhar, Punjab 144001. Consequently, the complainant presented the impugned cheque with its Banker, Citiy Bank, Central Market, West Punjabi Bagh, New Delhi which got dishonoured vide return memo dated 09.01.2019 with remarks "funds insufficient". 2. Thereafter, the complainant sent a legal demand notice dated 28.01.2019 on address of the accused. 3. Upon failure of the accused to make payment of the cheque in question within the stipulated time of 15 days, the complainant has filed the present complaint u/s 138 of the Act. 4. The complainant examined himself in presummoning evidence and after considering the complaint and entire documents on record, summon was issued by this Court against the accused on 08.05.2019. Notice against the accused: 5. Notice was framed against the accused on 12.03.2020 and the accused pleaded not guilty and claim trial. C.C. No.1727/19 Dated 17.01.2023 P Plea of defence of the accused: 6. The accused had taken the following plea in his defence: "I plead not guilty and claim trial. The cheque in question bears my signatures only. I received the legal demand notice in question from the complainant. The cheque in question was given as a blank signed security cheque to the complainant". 7. Thereafter, accused was permitted to crossexamine the complainant on 19.02.2021. Complainant's evidence: 8. The complainant examined himself as CW1 reiterating the statements made in the complaint. He also relied upon the documents Ex. CW1/1 to CW1/15. Board Resolution is Ex.CW1/1 Tax invoices are Ex. CW1/2 to Ex. CW1/5 Goods receipt are Ex. CW1/6 to Ex. CW1/8 Letter dated 27.12.2018 sent by the complainant to the accused alongwith original postal receipt and computer generated delivery report is Ex. CW1/9(colly) Ledger account of the complainant company is Ex.CW1/10 Original Return Memo Ex. CW1/12 Copy of legal 18. The Hon'Ble Supreme Court In Kumar ... vs . Sharma Carpets (2009) 2 Scc on 17 January, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/15751217/ 3 demand notice Ex.CW1/13 Original postal receipt Ex. CW1/14 Original acknowledgement card is Ex. CW1/15 Evidence by way of affidavit is Ex.CW1/A 9. Thereafter, CW1 was duly crossexamined by the Ld. Counsel of the accused. No other witness was examined by complainant. CE was closed by this Court vide order dated 01.04.2022. C.C. No.1727/19 Dated 17.01.2023 Pages Statement of the accused 10. Statement of the accused was recorded under section 313 Code of Criminal Procedure (hereinafter referred as "Cr.P.C") on 13.05.2022 wherein all the incriminating evidences were put up before the accused. 11. Accused stated that the cheque in question has given to the complainant against Form C in the year 201516. It was not against any liability and it was only issued for security purpose against Form C. He had already returned the goods to the complainant and that amount was not deducted against his liability. As on date he had no liability against the accused as all goods were returned which were near to expire and non saleble and puffed. The complainant misused the cheque which was given as security despite returning all goods. He had stop working with the complainant after returning of goods therefore as a tool of harassment and extortion, complainant used the cheque which was given as security, though he had no liability. Defence Evidence: 12. The accused examined himself as DW1. DE was closed by this court vide order dated 08.09.2022. 13. He also relied upon the following documents. Bank statement of accused company showing series of cheque is Ex. DW1/1(colly) Debit notes/Bills are Ex. DW1/2(colly) Photocopies of bilty/transport bills are Marked as Mark A(colly) Final arguments were heard on behalf of both the parties. The Law relating to Sec. 138 NI Act: 14.
texts.arguments: The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Krishna Janardhan Bhat v. Dattatraya G. Hegde AIR 2008 SC 1325 held that the procedural requirements of section 138 are: 18. The Hon'Ble Supreme Court In Kumar ... vs . Sharma Carpets (2009) 2 Scc on 17 January, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/15751217/ 4 The drawer of the cheque issued the cheque to satisfy part or whole of the debt. 18. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Kumar Exports vs. Sharma Carpets (2009) 2 SCC 513, while discussing the contours of section 118(a) r/w 139 of the N I Act, has held interalia the following: "14. Section 139 of the Act provides that it shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to in section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability. 15. Applying the definition of the word "proved" in section 3 of the Evidence Act to the provisions of sections 118 and 139 of the Act, it becomes evident that in a trial under section 138 of the Act a presumption will have to be made that every negotiable intstrument was made or drawn for consideration and that it was executed for discharge of debt or liability once the execution of negotiable instrument is either proved or admitted. A presumption is not in itself evidence, but only makes a prima facie case for a party for whose benefit it exists." 19. The Hon'Ble Supreme Court In Kumar ... vs . Sharma Carpets (2009) 2 Scc on 17 January, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/15751217/ 6 Blank signed cheque was given as security cheque as the date and figure in the cheque in question are filled with different ink. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in M.S Narayan Menon @ Mani vs. State of Kerala, Appeal (Crl) 1012 of 1999 has interalia held the following: "The standard of proof evidently is preponderance of probabilities. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials on record but also by reference to the circumstances upon which he relies" 23. Further, it should also be noted that the standard of proof in order to rebut the statutory presumption may be inferred from the materials on record and circumstantial evidences. At this point, reliance may be placed on the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Krishna Janardhan Bhat (supra), wherein the Hon'ble Court has categorically held the following: "32. accused for discharging the burden of proof placed upon him under a statute need not examine himself. He may discharge his burden on the basis of the materials already brought on record. As accused has a constitutional right to remain silence. 34. Furthermore, whereas prosecution must prove the guilt of an accused beyond all reasonable doubt, the standard of proof so as to prove defence on the part of an accused is "preponderance of probabilities". Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by the parties but also by reference to the circumstances upon which he relies." 18. The Hon'Ble Supreme Court In Kumar ... vs . Sharma Carpets (2009) 2 Scc on 17 January, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/15751217/ 7 24. This principle has been reiterated by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Rangappa vs. Sri Mohan (2010) 11 SCC 441 wherein while discussing the scope and ambit of statutory presumption under section 139 of the Act, the Hon'ble Court has held the following: C.C. No.1727/19 Dated 17.01.2023 Pages 9 "27. Section 139 of the Act is an example of a reverse onus clause that has been included in furtherance of the legislative objective of improving the credibility of negotiable instruments. While section 138 of the Act specifies a strong criminal remedy in relation to the dishonour of cheques, the rebuttable presumption under section 139 is a device to prevent undue delay in the course of litigation. In such a scenario, the test of proportionality should guide the construction and interpretation of reverse onus clauses and the defendantaccused cannot be expected to discharge an unduly high standard of proof. Reference can be taken from the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Bharat Barrel & Drum Manufacturing Company vs. Amin Chand Pyarelal 1999 (3) SCC 35, wherein it was held: "Upon consideration of various judgments as noted hereinabove, the position of law which emerges is that once execution of the promissory note is admitted, the presumption under section 118(a) C.C. No.1727/19 Dated 17.01.2023 Pages 10 would arise that it is supported by a consideration. Such a presumption is rebuttable. The defendant can prove the nonexistence of a consideration by raising a probable defence. The burden upon the defendant of proving 18. The Hon'Ble Supreme Court In Kumar ... vs . Sharma Carpets (2009) 2 Scc on 17 January, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/15751217/ 8 the non existence of the consideration can be either direct or by bringing on record preponderance of probabilities by reference to the circumstances upon which he relies. In case, where the defendant fails to discharge the initial onus of proof by showing the non existence of the consideration, the plaintiff would invariably be held entitled to the benefit of presumption arising under section 118(a) in his favour. Reference can be taken from the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of M/S Womb Laboratories Pvt Ltd vs Vijay Ahuja Criminal Appeals No. 13821383 of 2019 has categorically held that handing over of the cheques by way of security per se would not C.C. No.1727/19 Dated 17.01.2023 Pages 11 extricate the accused from the discharge of liability arising from such cheques. At this stage, I also find support from the decision of the Hon'ble Delhi High Court in the case of Suresh Chandra Goyal vs. Amit Singhal Crl. L.P 707/2014 wherein the Hon'ble Court has held the following: "28. There is no magic in the word "security cheque", such that, the moment the accused claims that the dishonoured cheque (in respect whereof a complaint under section 138 of the Act is preferred) was given as a "security cheque", the Magistrate would acquit the accused. The expression "security cheque" is not a statutorily defined expression in the NI Act. The NI Act does not per se carve out an exception in respect of a 'security cheque' to say that a complaint in respect of such a cheque would not be maintainable." 28. Further, Ld. Counsel for the accused argues that the date and figure are filled with different ink which shows that the same was not filled by the accused. Moreover, Ld. Counsel for the accused contends that the cheque was issued in the year 2015 against Form C. The Hon'Ble Supreme Court In Kumar ... vs . Sharma Carpets (2009) 2 Scc on 17 January, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/15751217/ 9 that if the accused is issuing a cheque after signing the same to the complaint albeit blank, he is giving implied authority to the complainant to fill the blank details and to present the cheque on or after the date mentioned in the cheque. 29. Reference can be taken from the recent decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Bir Singh vs. Mukesh Kumar (2019) 4 SCC 197 wherein the Apex Court while upholding the validity of blank signed cheque and post dated cheque in a proceeding u/s 138 of the Act has interalia held the following: "36. 37. A meaningful reading of the provisions of the Negotiable Instruments Act including, in particular, Sections 20, 87 and 139, makes it amply clear that a person who signs a cheque and makes it over to the payee remains liable unless he adduces evidence to rebut the presumption that the cheque had been issued for payment of a debt or in discharge of a liability. It is immaterial that the cheque may have been filled in by any person other than the drawer, if the cheque is duly signed by the drawer. 38. If a signed blank cheque is voluntarily presented to a payee,towards some payment, the payee may fill up the amount and other particulars. The onus would still be on the accused to prove that the cheque was not in discharge of a debt or liability by adducing evidence." 30. Further, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Sampelly Satyanarayan Rao vs. Indian Renewable Energy (2016) 10 SCC 458 while discussing the ambit of section 138 of the Act visavis a cheque which has been stated to be given as security for repayment of loan, had interalia held the following: "We are of the view that the question whether a postdated cheque is for "discharge of debt or liability" depends on the nature of the transaction. If on the date of the cheque liability or debt exists or the amount has become legally recoverable, the Section is attracted and not otherwise. Reference to the facts of the present case clearly shows that though the word "security" is used in clause 3.1(iii) of the agreement, the said expression refers to the cheques being towards repayment of 18. The Hon'Ble Supreme Court In Kumar ... vs . Sharma Carpets (2009) 2 Scc on 17 January, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/15751217/ 10 installments. The repayment becomes due under the agreement, the moment the loan is advanced and the installment falls due. It is undisputed that the loan was duly disbursed on 28th February, 2002 which was prior to the date of the cheques. Once the loan was disbursed and installments have fallen due on the date of the cheque as per the agreement, dishonour of such cheques would fall under Section 138 of the Act. The cheques undoubtedly represent the outstanding liability." 31. Reference can also be taken from the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of ICDS vs. Beena Shabeer AIR 2002 SC 3014 wherein the Hon'ble Court has discussed the contours of section 138 of the Act in order to include in its ambit "any cheque" C.C. No.1727/19 Dated 17.01.2023 Pages 13 issued in discharge of debt or other liability. Relevant extract of the judgment is reproduced below: "The language, however, has been rather specific as regards the intent of the legislature. The commencement of the Section stands with the words "Where any cheque". Any contra interpretation would defeat the intent of the legislature" 32. The Hon'Ble Supreme Court In Kumar ... vs . Sharma Carpets (2009) 2 Scc on 17 January, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/15751217/ 11 legally enforceable debt C.C. No.1727/19 Dated 17.01.2023 Pages 14 on the date when the said cheque was issued. It is for the accused to prove that no legally enforceable debt existed on the date on which the cheque was issued. Counsel for the accused argues that the accused and the complainant are in the business of perishable food products and the complainant sold damaged and expired goods to the accused which is against the guidelines of the FSSAI. Further, the goods were duly returned by the accused, however, the complainant did not adjust the amount of returned goods. Counsel for the complainant contends that some goods were returned by accused in the month of October, 2018. (1) If a food business operator considers or has reasons to believe that a food which he has processed, manufactured or distributed is not in compliance with this Act, or the rules or regulations, made thereunder, he shall immediately initiate procedures to withdraw the food in question from the market and consumers indicating reasons for its withdrawal and inform the competent authorities thereof". C.C. No.1727/19 Dated 17.01.2023 Pages 15 37. When goods are delivered to the buyer on approval or "on sale or return" or other similar terms, the property therein passes to the buyer (a) when he signifies his approval or acceptance to the seller or does any other act adopting the transaction; (b) if he does not signify his approval or acceptance to the seller but retains the goods without giving notice of rejection, then, if a time has been fixed for the return of the goods, on the expiration of such time, and, if no time has been fixed, on the expiration of a reasonable time. Section 26. Risk prima facie passes with property.
